passages.title: Honey Bees
passages.body: Honey bees are among the most industrious insects on Earth. A single hive may contain up to sixty thousand bees, yet each one has a clearly defined role. Worker bees, all female, gather nectar and pollen, while the single queen lays all the eggs. As bees move from flower to flower collecting nectar, they transfer pollen, allowing plants to reproduce. Scientists estimate that nearly one-third of the food we eat depends on such pollination. In recent years, however, bee populations have declined sharply, alarming farmers and ecologists alike.

passages.title: The Printing Press
passages.body: Before the fifteenth century, books in Europe were copied by hand, a slow and costly process that kept reading a privilege of the wealthy few. Around 1440, Johannes Gutenberg introduced a printing press that used movable metal type. Suddenly, identical copies of a text could be produced quickly and cheaply. Within decades, printed books spread across the continent, carrying new ideas far beyond the walls of monasteries and palaces. Literacy rose, and knowledge that had once been guarded by a small elite became available to ordinary people. Many historians regard this invention as one of the most influential in human history.

passages.title: Plastic in the Oceans
passages.body: Every year, millions of tonnes of plastic waste end up in the oceans. Unlike natural materials, most plastics do not decompose; instead they break into ever-smaller fragments called microplastics. These particles are swallowed by fish and other marine creatures, and eventually make their way up the food chain to humans. Governments have begun to ban single-use plastic bags and straws, but critics argue that such steps are far too small. Real change, they insist, will require redesigning how products are packaged and how waste is managed. Until then, the tide of plastic shows no sign of turning.

passages.title: The Red Kite
passages.body: Arjun had waited all week for a windy day. On Sunday morning, clutching his new red kite, he ran to the open field behind his house. For nearly an hour the kite refused to rise, dipping and crashing into the grass. Just as he was about to give up, a strong gust lifted it high into the sky. Arjun laughed aloud, forgetting his sore arms and the long hour of failure. That evening he told his sister that the best moments are often the ones you almost miss.

passages.title: Everyday AI
passages.body: Artificial intelligence has quietly woven itself into everyday life. When a phone suggests the next word in a message, recommends a song, or recognises a face in a photograph, it is using machine learning. These systems improve by studying vast amounts of data rather than by following fixed rules written by programmers. Their convenience is undeniable, yet they raise difficult questions about privacy and fairness. If a system learns from biased data, it may repeat those biases in its decisions. As AI takes on larger roles, society will have to decide how much trust such systems deserve.

passages.title: The Water Cycle
passages.body: The water on Earth is constantly on the move, endlessly recycled through the water cycle. Heat from the sun causes water in oceans, rivers, and lakes to evaporate into vapour. As this vapour rises and cools, it condenses into tiny droplets that form clouds. When the droplets grow heavy enough, they fall back to the surface as rain or snow, a process called precipitation. Some of this water flows into rivers and returns to the sea, while some soaks into the ground. In this way, the same water has circulated for billions of years.
